Louisville property tax is billed by the offices named below.

Who bills what in Louisville

  • Jefferson County Property Valuation Administrator handles assessment.
  • Jefferson County Sheriff's Office bills and collects the tax.

Due dates

Page states 2026 tax bills are mailed in November and payable to the Jefferson County Sheriff's Office from November 1, 2026 through April 15, 2027. Discount/penalty schedule not on the opened page.. See the official page.

Challenging your assessment

2026 PVA Online Conference window opened April 24, 2026 noon EDT and closed May 18, 2026 4pm EDT; the Online Conference is the required first step, then a hearing with the Local Board of Assessment Appeals (filed with the Jefferson County Clerk per PVA resources page excerpt). Owners need not receive a notice to appeal.. See the official page.

We could not confirm the current Louisville rate on an opened page, so we do not state one.

Local notes

  • Assessment appeals: PVA conference first, then county clerk filing, then local Board of Assessment Appeals (KDOR 62F003 opened).

Louisville by the numbers

The Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey counts about 627,210 people in Louisville, which makes it the 1st largest of the 16 ky places we cover. The median value of an owner-occupied home is $221,500, 6% above the median of those 16 places. 61% of occupied homes are owner-occupied and 39% are rented, against a median of 54% owner-occupancy across the ky places. The median home was built in 1970, about 53 years ago, which matters for roofs, plumbing and inspection requests. These numbers describe Louisville as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Which offices handle Louisville property tax?

The Jefferson County Sheriff bills Louisville's property tax. Louisville and Jefferson County have shared the same borders since 2003 under the Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Government, so one set of county offices serves the whole merged area. Four of them touch a typical Louisville bill.

Offices that value, bill and collect property tax for Louisville addresses
OfficeJobLocation and phone
Jefferson County PVAValues property, grants exemptions, holds conferencesGlassworks Building, 815 W. Market St., Suite 400; 502-574-6380
Jefferson County Sheriff, Property Tax DepartmentCollects current-year billsFiscal Court Building, 700 W. Liberty St.; 502-574-5479
Jefferson County ClerkHolds delinquent bills after April 15527 W. Jefferson St., Suite 100a; 502-574-5884
Jefferson County Attorney, Tax DivisionRuns payment plans for delinquent taxFirst Trust Centre, 200 S. Fifth St., Suite 200N; 502-574-6331

The Sheriff's counter takes payments on weekdays, 8 AM to 4 PM. Mailed payments go to PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570.

What does the Louisville tax bill pay for?

One Sheriff's bill funds up to 13 taxing jurisdictions, and the office reports about $1 billion collected a year from more than 300,000 taxpayers. The Sheriff's published list shows how many layers sit on a Louisville house.

  • The Commonwealth of Kentucky and the Jefferson County Board of Education.
  • Louisville/Jefferson County Metro Government and the Urban-Service District.
  • The Louisville Downtown Management District, for parcels inside it.
  • A fire protection district, such as Okolona, Fern Creek, Fairdale, Pleasure Ridge Park, Jeffersontown/McMahan, St. Matthews/Lyndon, or Anchorage/Middletown.

The Jefferson County PVA counts 83 incorporated taxing jurisdictions covering about 60,000 properties, and many of these smaller home rule cities send a separate bill. If your address lies in a suburban city, call that city's clerk about rates and amounts, since that bill is in addition to the Sheriff's. The PVA website carries a contact list for each city.

What is Louisville like for someone selling a house?

Louisville is a river city that grew around a portage, and its housing stock reflects more than two centuries of growth. The settlement was founded in 1778 beside the Falls of the Ohio, and the city is now the most populous in Kentucky, with a Census Bureau 2025 estimate of 641,962 residents for the metro government's balance area.

The Ohio River shaped both the map and the market. In January 1937 the river crested at 57.15 feet, almost 30 feet above flood stage, and water covered 60 to 70 percent of the city. Afterward, residential growth shifted to higher ground in the east, and floodwalls now protect the low areas. Downtown sits south of the river, the airport is about 6.75 miles south of downtown, and industry clusters south and west of the airport.

Greater Louisville Association of Realtors data, as summarized on Wikipedia, shows the lowest median sale prices west of Interstate 65 in the West and South Ends and the highest north of Interstate 64 in the East End. Older neighborhoods around Old Louisville, Bardstown Road, Frankfort Avenue and NuLu were revived beginning in the 1980s. Weather matters too: the climate is humid subtropical, severe storms and occasional tornado outbreaks are part of the record, and winter can bring ice that damages roofs and trees.

What do Census numbers show about Louisville homes?

For the metro government's balance area, the 2020 to 2024 survey reports a median home value of $233,900 among owner-occupied houses, and owners live in 60.7 percent of occupied homes, so about two in five households rent. Median gross rent is $1,120 a month and median household income is $66,849. The typical commute takes 22.5 minutes. Households number 264,505, and 33.8 percent of adults over 25 hold a bachelor's degree or more.

Averages hide the district differences. The same assessed value can carry a different bill in a fire district or a home rule city than in the Urban-Service District, so read the district lines on your own bill.

When does Louisville property tax come due?

Bills are mailed by November 1 and rest on the assessed value as of January 1. For 2026, the County Attorney's page says the Sheriff takes payment from November 1, 2026 through April 15, 2027.

  • November 1 to December 1: 2 percent discount.
  • December 2 to January 4: face amount.
  • January 5 to February 5: 5 percent penalty.
  • February 6 to April 15: 10 percent penalty plus a 10 percent Sheriff's add-on.

A deadline that falls on a weekend or Sheriff's Office holiday shifts to the following business day. If no bill has come by the second week of November, call 502-574-5479 for a duplicate, because a missing bill does not waive penalties.

You can pay with cash, check or money order at the counter, by mail, in drop boxes at several County Clerk branches (Dixie, Fairdale, Highview, East and Westport), or through an online portal. Online fees run $2.00 for an eCheck and 2.25 percent for cards, and the Sheriff's Office keeps none of it. Partial payments are accepted on the current-year bill during collection.

What is the route to a lower Louisville assessment?

Use the PVA Online Conference during the annual inspection period, then take the dispute to the Local Board of Assessment Appeals through the County Clerk. For 2026 the online conference opened April 24 at noon and closed May 18 at 4 pm, a longer run than the 13 days that state law requires beginning early in May.

  • Evidence helps: photographs, an appraisal, an insurance policy, repair estimates, construction costs, or a listing contract.
  • Comparable sales should be arm's-length transactions, and for homes within two years of the assessment date. The PVA discards foreclosures, short sales and family sales.
  • A phone conference is available at 502-574-6224, with supporting papers due at least 3 days earlier.

The board petition goes to the County Clerk by the workday after the inspection period ends, or by the date on your online conference result. Three people sit on the board: two named by the Mayor of Louisville Metro and one by Metro Council. The clerk's appeals line is 502-574-6915. A result you still dispute can go on to the state tax appeals board.

What help exists when a Louisville owner cannot pay?

The best option depends on when the bill turns late. Seniors and totally disabled owners can apply at the PVA for the $49,100 homestead exemption that applies to the 2025 and 2026 assessment years.

The Jefferson County Attorney's Tax Division sets up payment plans for delinquent bills. Plans for 2025 taxes opened on April 16, 2026, and 2026 bills are not eligible until April 26, 2027. An owner behind on an earlier plan must catch up before 2025 can be added, and a written request may win a waiver of certain penalties and fees under 103 KAR 1:040. A bill on a payment plan cannot be sold at the tax sale.

In nine West End neighborhoods (Algonquin, California, Chickasaw, Park DuValle, Parkhill, Parkland, Portland, Russell and Shawnee), LHOME and the West End Opportunity Partnership offer a grant or 0 percent loan so qualifying residents can keep a residential bill current. Their number is 502-882-8091.

What happens to unpaid Louisville property tax when I sell?

A bill unpaid after April 15 turns into a certificate of delinquency, a lien of record on the house. The County Attorney says approximately 40 percent in fees, interest and penalties is added at that point, and the certificate then earns interest at 12 percent a year. Unpaid certificates can be sold to a third party, and collection can include foreclosure.

At closing, the seller usually pays the prorated tax for the months owned, and the buyer pays the whole bill. The name on the official roll cannot be changed mid-year, so a new owner pays a bill printed in the prior owner's name. A change-of-address form sent to the PVA covers future bills. If an outside investor bought the certificate, the clerk's online records will show it, and payment goes to the investor.

More questions about Louisville, KY Property Tax Guide

Who receives Louisville property tax payments?

The Jefferson County Sheriff's Office takes them at 700 W. Liberty St., by mail at PO Box 34570, Louisville, KY 40232-4570, or online. After April 15 the bill shifts to the Jefferson County Clerk. Smaller home rule cities send their own bill.

Does paying early save money on a Louisville bill?

Yes, 2 percent when you pay between November 1 and December 1. The face amount is due December 2 through January 4, then penalties begin.

Is there a second, city-level property tax bill in Louisville?

For most addresses the answer is no, because the Sheriff's bill covers Louisville Metro and the Urban-Service District. An address inside one of the 83 smaller incorporated cities in the county gets an extra bill from that city.

How do I contest my Louisville assessment?

Complete the PVA Online Conference during the inspection period, which begins in early May. If the result does not satisfy you, file with the Jefferson County Clerk for a Local Board of Assessment Appeals hearing by the workday after the period ends.

Can delinquent Louisville property tax go on a payment plan?

Yes. The Jefferson County Attorney's Tax Division arranges plans at 502-574-6331. Current-year bills qualify only after they become delinquent, and a bill on a plan cannot be sold at the tax sale.

Who bills what in Lexington

  • Fayette County Property Valuation Administrator handles assessment.
  • Fayette County Sheriff's Office bills and collects the tax.

Due dates

2026 bills: 10/01/2026-11/01/2026 2% discount; 11/02-12/31/2026 face amount; 01/01-01/31/2027 5% penalty; 02/01-04/15/2027 10% penalty + 10% add-on (page lists 2026 bills mailed last week of Sept 2026).. See the official page.

Local notes

  • Assessment appeals: PVA conference first, then county clerk filing, then local Board of Assessment Appeals (KDOR 62F003 opened).
  • Many Kentucky cities bill and collect their own city property tax separately from the county Sheriff bill; see each city's notes.
  • Census Vintage 2025 population 329751; county Fayette County.

Get My Cash Offer →

Lexington by the numbers

Lexington has roughly 321,122 residents in the Census Bureau's 2019-2023 survey, and ranks number 2 by population among the 16 ky places in this guide. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $272,100 here, which is 31% above the middle figure for the 16 ky places. About 46% of households rent, so 54% own; the ky median for these places is 54% owner-occupied. Homes here were typically built in 1983, so the median house is about 40 years old. These numbers describe Lexington as a whole, so a given street can sit well above or below them.

Does the city of Lexington send its own property tax bill?

No separate city bill exists, because Lexington and Fayette County operate as one government. The Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government (LFUCG) replaced the separate city and county governments in the early 1970s, when police and fire services were merged, and the Fayette County Sheriff collects property tax for the whole territory. The Fayette County PVA, which values every parcel, says on its rate page that the total bill is built from rates set by the Commonwealth, the LFUCG, Fayette County Public Schools and a few other districts.

What differs from one Lexington address to the next is the service district. Seven residential districts appear on the PVA's 2026 chart, and each pays the same base lines for state, schools, general services, the extension office, soil conservation, public health, Lextran buses and parks. Only the curbside extras separate them.

  • The full-service district adds 17.3 cents per $100 for trash pickup, street lights and street cleaning.
  • Districts with only refuse add 13.7 cents, only street lights 2.7 cents, and combinations fall in between.
  • The school line is the biggest piece of every bill at 79.7 cents per $100, about 63 percent of the full-service total of $1.2598.

On a home assessed at $300,000, the gap between the full-service district and the district without optional services is $519 a year. Find the district number on your bill or ask the PVA, because it changes what a buyer will pay each month.

How do blighted-property and downtown charges change a Lexington bill?

Two surcharges apply only in certain places. When the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission labels a parcel abandoned and blighted, the owner pays $1 more per $100 of taxable value. On a $200,000 assessment, that is $2,000 a year on top of the normal bill, which makes a neglected vacant house expensive to hold. A parcel inside the Downtown Lexington Management District pays an extra 10 cents per $100.

Owners of empty houses should learn whether the commission has certified theirs before listing. The LFUCG can tell you, and a buyer will price the surcharge into any offer.

Why does Lexington's Urban Service Area matter to a seller?

In 1958 Lexington became the first American city to adopt an urban growth boundary. Inside it, in the urban service area, development could proceed at city density. Outside, in the rural service area, parcels had to be at least 40 acres, a rule meant to shield the horse farms around town. A 1980 plan update added urban and rural activity centers, the rural ones clustered around the I-64 and I-75 interchanges. The boundary was widened in 1996 by 5,300 acres, and in 2000 the city adopted a purchase-of-development-rights program that received $40 million in 2001, made of $25 million from local sources and $15 million from the state.

For a seller, the line decides which kind of parcel you have. Property outside it can sit on a large lot in farm use, and Kentucky assesses farmland at agricultural value instead of market value, which changes the tax math completely. Pull the parcel record from the PVA to confirm the tax district and land use before pricing. Expect different answers for a subdivision lot inside the line and for acreage outside it.

How big has Lexington grown?

The consolidated city spans 285.5 square miles, almost all of it land. Its metro area reaches into Clark, Jessamine, Bourbon, Woodford and Scott counties, held 516,811 people in 2020, and ranks second in Kentucky behind Louisville. Adding Richmond and Frankfort gives a combined area of 747,919. A party of frontiersmen under William McConnell camped at the site in June 1775 and named it for Lexington, Massachusetts, after hearing of the fighting there. Forty-five settlers signed the Lexington Compact on January 25, 1780.

The jump from 108,137 to 204,165 across the 1970s came in the same decade that the city and county governments merged. Since 1990 each decade has added between 9 and 16 percent.

What should I know about Lexington's schools, roads and weather before listing?

The Lexington entry on Wikipedia describes a Fayette County Public Schools system of six district high schools, 12 middle schools and 37 elementary schools, with many private schools on top of that. The University of Kentucky and Transylvania University are the two traditional colleges, and Blue Grass Airport is on the west side along US 60. I-75 skirts the city and I-64 runs along the north. US 25, 27, 60, 68 and 421 meet in Lexington, which has few freeways and a reputation for congestion.

Weather is moderate and fairly wet. A typical year brings about 49.8 inches of precipitation, 14.5 inches of snow, 25 days of 90-degree heat and 23 winter days that stay below freezing. The Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America also rates the area as high-allergy.

What happens to unpaid Lexington property tax?

Once a bill is delinquent, the Fayette County Clerk is the office to deal with, and its rules are rigid. A delinquent bill is a lien, so the clerk wants certified funds. Interest raises the balance each month.

  • Accepted: cash, a money order, or a cashier's or certified check payable to the Fayette County Clerk.
  • Turned away: personal checks, business checks, counter checks and credit cards.
  • Not available: partial payments on a delinquent bill.

Owners who cannot pay in full can phone the Fayette County Attorney's Office at 859-254-4941 to ask about a payment arrangement.

Visit Room 132 at 162 E. Main Street, Lexington, KY 40507, or call 859-253-3344 during payoff hours of 8:00 to 4:30. The clerk's deeds website has a search tool and a calculator. Every year the clerk sells eligible delinquent bills to third-party purchasers between 90 and 135 days after the sheriff's handoff. The 2026 sale was held July 24 at 11:00 a.m., and registration details for 2027 are due in spring 2027. A seller should obtain the payoff before the listing goes live.

What do Lexington sellers owe when the deed is recorded?

Selling a house here triggers the state transfer tax in KRS 142.050: $0.50 for each $500 of price, with any leftover fraction counted as a full unit. A $325,000 sale produces $325. The grantor bears it, and the Fayette County Clerk computes it and collects before the deed can be filed. Foreclosure transfers, transfers between spouses in a divorce, and parent-to-child transfers for nominal consideration are exempt.

Property tax runs on a separate track. Whoever held title at the start of the year gets the bill, and the contract or settlement statement says how the cost is divided. A seller who is 65 or disabled may be receiving the $49,100 homestead exemption in force for 2025 and 2026, but a buyer must file a new application with the Fayette County PVA.

More questions about Lexington, KY Property Tax Guide

Is there a separate city property tax in Lexington?

No. Lexington and Fayette County share one urban county government, so the single bill from the Fayette County Sheriff covers state, school, county and urban-government charges. Rates depend on the service district of your address.

What is the biggest part of a Lexington tax bill?

The school line. On the PVA's 2026 chart it is 79.7 cents per $100 in each residential district, set against a full-service total of $1.2598.

How much extra does a blighted Lexington property pay?

An extra $1 per $100 of taxable value once the LFUCG Vacant Property Review Commission certifies it as abandoned and blighted. On a $200,000 assessment that is $2,000 a year.

Can I pay delinquent Lexington tax with a credit card?

No. The Fayette County Clerk takes only cash, money orders and cashier's or certified checks for delinquent bills, and it does not accept partial payments.

What is the Lexington transfer tax on a home sale?

Under KRS 142.050 the seller pays $0.50 per $500 of price at recording, so a $325,000 sale carries a $325 charge, collected by the Fayette County Clerk.
